name: Antiperspirant

chain: Drier clothes, less odor, fresher presence
angle.text: Antiperspirants reduce underarm sweat with aluminium salts, keeping shirts dry and cutting the moisture odor-causing bacteria feed on. It is the everyday hygiene staple in grooming routines, and sweat reduction is measurable.

summary: Aluminium-salt sweat blockers, the everyday wetness and odor fix.
note: Breast cancer and Alzheimer's concerns have been studied; reviews cited report no reliable link.
currentQuick:
Antiperspirants reduce underarm sweating using aluminium salts, unlike deodorants which target odor. They are sold in sticks, roll-ons, sprays and gels.
They are among the most common grooming products, and stronger versions are used for excessive sweating.
How it works: Aluminium salts react with sweat and form temporary plugs in sweat ducts, with a mild astringent effect, so less sweat reaches the skin surface.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are skin irritation, and zirconium products can cause granulomas. The FDA advises people with kidney problems to consult a doctor. Breast cancer and Alzheimer's claims have been studied; reviews summarized on Wikipedia found little or no reliable evidence of a link.
deepLead:
An antiperspirant is a topical product that reduces sweating, most commonly using aluminium salts such as aluminium chlorohydrate. It differs from a deodorant, which targets odor rather than sweat output. In the United States antiperspirants are regulated as over-the-counter drugs, whereas deodorants are cosmetics; in the European Union antiperspirants are generally classed as cosmetics.
In appearance culture, antiperspirants are used to control wetness, sweat marks and odor. Aluminium salts are thought to form temporary plugs in sweat-gland ducts, reducing the sweat that reaches the skin surface. The same ingredient family at higher strengths is used for hyperhidrosis. Public concerns about links to breast cancer and Alzheimer's disease have been examined in studies; reviews summarized by Wikipedia report no reliable evidence of a link.

name: Deodorant

angle.text: Deodorants are applied to the underarms to control body odor, the basic scent-hygiene step in grooming, on the premise that smell affects perceived attractiveness. Odor control is immediately noticeable, though claims like skipping soap for an ideal scent are anecdotal.

summary: Odor control, not sweat control; the basic scent-hygiene tool.
note: Does not reduce sweating; that is what antiperspirants do.
currentQuick:
Deodorants control body odor by masking scent or limiting odor-causing bacteria. They do not reduce sweat.
Forum users discuss them as part of scent and hygiene.
How it works: Underarm bacteria break down sweat to produce odor. Deodorants use fragrance, alcohol, alum or antimicrobials to mask or inhibit this.
Risks and caveats: Possible skin irritation or dermatitis from some ingredients, and cold burns from aerosols held close. Ingredients such as triclosan and phthalates have been studied for exposure.
deepLead:
A deodorant is a product applied to the skin, usually the underarms, to control body odor. It does not stop sweating, unlike an antiperspirant. Odor arises mainly when skin bacteria break down sweat, especially apocrine secretions that become active at puberty.
Deodorants work by masking odor with fragrance, absorbing moisture, or inhibiting bacteria with ingredients such as alcohol, triclosan or alum crystals. In the US they are regulated as cosmetics. In looksmaxxing forums, deodorant and fragrance are discussed as part of scent and hygiene.

name: Clinical strength antiperspirant

angle.text: Heavy sweaters use these stronger over-the-counter antiperspirants as a step before prescription options, to keep clothing dry and underarms fresh. Topical antiperspirants are listed as first-line care for hyperhidrosis in guidelines.

summary: Stronger-aluminium antiperspirants for heavy sweaters; a step before Rx.
note: Irritation is the most common side effect.
currentQuick:
Clinical strength antiperspirants contain more aluminium salt than regular ones and target heavy sweating.
Sources found on branded products are thin.
How it works: Aluminium salts plug sweat ducts so less sweat reaches the skin.
Risks and caveats: Skin irritation is the most common effect. People with kidney dysfunction are advised by the FDA to consult a doctor first.
deepLead:
Clinical strength antiperspirants are over-the-counter antiperspirants sold with higher concentrations of aluminium salts than ordinary products, aimed at people with heavy sweating. Ordinary antiperspirants use aluminium salts to form temporary plugs in sweat ducts, and topical antiperspirants are listed as first-line treatment for hyperhidrosis in guidelines.
Hyperhidrosis treatment with stronger aluminium chloride products is described as taking about three to five days to show improvement, with skin irritation as the most common side effect. Evidence specific to branded clinical strength products was not found in the sources loaded.

name: Aluminum chloride prescription (Drysol)

chain: Strong aluminium chloride blocks sweat ducts
angle.text: Prescription aluminium chloride is used for heavy sweating, to stay dry and avoid visible sweat marks and odor. Guidelines list topical antiperspirants as first-line therapy, and the product is established for hyperhidrosis.

summary: Rx aluminium chloride for heavy sweating; first-line, mainly irritating.
note: Skin irritation is the most common side effect.
currentQuick:
Drysol is a prescription aluminium chloride solution used for hyperhidrosis. It is a stronger form of the ingredient in ordinary antiperspirants.
Topical antiperspirants are guideline first-line treatment.
How it works: Aluminium salts block sweat ducts, reducing sweat output.
Risks and caveats: Skin irritation is the most common effect. Kidney dysfunction warrants a doctor consult per the FDA.
deepLead:
Drysol is a brand of prescription topical aluminium chloride solution used for hyperhidrosis, or excessive sweating. Aluminium chloride is a stronger version of the ingredient in regular antiperspirants, and guidelines list topical antiperspirants as first-line therapy.
Wikipedia reports that improvement takes about three to five days and that the most common side effect is skin irritation. In appearance culture it matters mainly to people concerned with visible underarm, hand or foot sweat.

name: Botox for underarm sweat

angle.text: Clinic-delivered botulinum toxin injections switch off underarm sweat glands for months, appealing to people who want dry clothes and less odor. It is studied for axillary hyperhidrosis, with limited research on its use for odor specifically.

summary: Neurotoxin injections that switch off underarm sweat glands for months at a time, a clinician-delivered option with thin entry-specific research.
note: Effect is temporary and requires repeat injections.
currentQuick:
Botox for underarm sweat means injecting botulinum toxin into the armpit skin to reduce sweating. It is described in reference sources as an approved option for severe underarm sweating that topical products have not controlled.
The effect is reported to last about 3 to 9 months, after which injections are repeated.
How it works: The toxin blocks release of acetylcholine from nerve endings, so the nerves stop signalling sweat glands to produce sweat.
Risks and caveats: Injections can be painful. General botulinum toxin warnings include spread of effect to nearby muscles. The effect wears off and treatment is repeated.
deepLead:
Botulinum toxin injections for underarm sweat involve injecting a neurotoxin into the skin of the armpit to reduce excessive sweating (axillary hyperhidrosis). The toxin blocks the release of acetylcholine from nerve endings, which is the signal that tells sweat glands to produce sweat .
Reference sources describe the treatment as an approved option for severe underarm sweating that topical agents have not controlled, with effects reported to last roughly 3 to 9 months before repeat injections are needed . Injections can be painful, and ice is sometimes used to reduce discomfort .
In looksmaxxing and grooming discussions it is grouped with other methods for reducing visible sweat and odor. Published clinical research specific to this entry in the available record is limited to a small registered trial combining botulinum toxin with suction-curettage .

name: miraDry

angle.text: miraDry is a clinic microwave treatment aimed at long-lasting reduction of underarm sweat and odor. It is FDA-cleared for axillary hyperhidrosis and studied in several trials, and its odor use is a secondary indication.

summary: A microwave device that destroys underarm sweat glands in a clinic; studied in several trials, with rare but serious nerve-injury and infection case reports.
note: Case reports document brachial plexus injury and one fatal infection.
currentQuick:
miraDry is an FDA-cleared microwave device used in clinics to destroy underarm sweat glands, mainly for heavy sweating and sometimes odor. Treatment is done under local anesthetic.
Several registered trials, patient surveys and a three-year follow-up have been published, alongside case reports of complications.
How it works: Microwave energy heats the tissue layer containing sweat glands, destroying them so they stop producing sweat.
Risks and caveats: Case reports describe brachial plexus (nerve) injury, and one fatal necrotizing fasciitis case. Authors have discussed a nerve-injury 'danger zone' and pretreatment assessment.
deepLead:
miraDry is a non-invasive microwave device made by Miramar Labs that heats tissue in the armpit to destroy sweat glands. It has been cleared by the US FDA and Health Canada for axillary hyperhidrosis and is also used for underarm odor .
Treatment typically involves local anesthetic injection into the armpit followed by application of the microwave emitter to the skin . A 2022 review of microwave technology in dermatology covers its use for axillary hyperhidrosis and osmidrosis among other conditions .
Several clinical studies and a patient survey have been published, and case reports document rare serious complications including brachial plexus nerve injury and a fatal infection .

name: Axillary sweat gland suction

angle.text: This minor surgery removes or disrupts underarm sweat glands for people seeking lasting dryness and less odor. Evidence in our sources comes from small registered trials.

summary: Surgical removal of underarm sweat glands through small incisions, with only small registered trials behind it in our sources.
note: Surgical procedure; outcome data in available sources are sparse.
currentQuick:
Axillary sweat gland suction is a minor surgery in which armpit sweat glands are removed or disrupted using suction or curettage. It is used for heavy underarm sweating and sometimes for underarm odor.
Only small registered trials appear in the available record, without published results.
How it works: Physically removing or destroying the glands means they can no longer produce sweat.
Risks and caveats: Surgical risks apply in general; specific complication data were not available in the reviewed sources.
deepLead:
Axillary sweat gland suction, also called suction-curettage or liposuction-type removal, is a minor surgical approach to underarm sweating in which sweat glands in the armpit are physically removed or disrupted through small incisions .
Wikipedia's hyperhidrosis article lists axillary sweat gland removal or destruction by suction, curettage, liposuction-type removal or laser ablation among surgical options . Related procedures are also used for underarm odor (osmidrosis) .
The available record contains two small registered trials and no published results summaries, so evidence for this entry in this wiki is limited to what those registrations describe.

name: Glycopyrronium wipes (Qbrexza)

angle.text: Prescription glycopyrronium wipes are applied to the underarms to cut excessive sweating and keep clothes dry. The FDA approved topical glycopyrronium for primary axillary hyperhidrosis in 2018, so the sweat effect is studied.

summary: Prescription anticholinergic wipes for underarm sweat, FDA-approved in 2018, with case reports of accidental pupil dilation in children.
note: Case reports of pupil dilation in children after accidental exposure.
currentQuick:
Qbrexza wipes contain glycopyrronium, an anticholinergic, and are wiped on the underarms to reduce sweating. The FDA approved topical glycopyrronium for primary axillary hyperhidrosis in June 2018.
It is prescription-only.
How it works: Glycopyrronium blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, reducing the nerve signal that triggers sweat glands.
Risks and caveats: Anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth and blurred vision are listed for glycopyrronium. Case reports describe pupil dilation in infants and children after accidental exposure.
deepLead:
Glycopyrronium tosylate wipes, sold as Qbrexza, are single-use cloths containing a topical anticholinergic, applied to the underarms to reduce excessive sweating. The US FDA approved topical glycopyrronium for primary axillary hyperhidrosis in June 2018 .
Glycopyrronium is a peripherally selective antimuscarinic that blocks muscarinic receptors and so inhibits cholinergic signalling to sweat glands . Wikipedia describes the 2018 approval as the first drug developed specifically to reduce excessive sweating .
Published case reports describe unintended spread of the drug to the eyes of children, producing pupil dilation .

name: Oxybutynin for sweating

chain: Dry skin and clothes, less odor
angle.text: Oxybutynin is a bladder drug used off-label to reduce excessive sweating, so users can stay dry and avoid sweat marks. A placebo-controlled trial supports the sweat reduction; the appearance benefit is a side use of the drug.

summary: A bladder drug used off-label as a sweat blocker, with a placebo-controlled trial behind it and a full anticholinergic side-effect profile.
note: Off-label for sweating; anticholinergic side effects include heat stroke risk.
currentQuick:
Oxybutynin is a prescription anticholinergic drug approved for overactive bladder and prescribed off-label for excessive sweating. A 2012 double-blind trial reported reduced sweating in sertraline-treated patients.
As of 2024 its use for sweating remains off-label.
How it works: It blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, reducing the signal that activates sweat glands.
Risks and caveats: Dry mouth, constipation, dizziness, urinary retention, heat stroke and delirium are listed; a large study linked cumulative anticholinergic use to dementia risk in people over 65.
deepLead:
Oxybutynin is an anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) medication approved in the US in 1975 for overactive bladder. It is also used off-label to reduce excessive sweating, increasingly since the 2010s .
Wikipedia notes that, as of 2024, this use remains off-label because dosing and the full side-effect profile are not established . Reference sources list oral anticholinergics such as oxybutynin among treatments for focal and generalized hyperhidrosis, with side effects including dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation and vision changes .
Published studies include a double-blind placebo-controlled trial in depressed patients on sertraline, and several registered studies in hyperhidrosis .

name: Iontophoresis

chain: Sweat glands in palms and soles quieted
angle.text: Iontophoresis uses a low electric current to treat sweaty palms and soles, helping people keep hands dry and feet less odorous. It has been used since the 1950s for hyperhidrosis, and its role in appearance is mainly dryness.

summary: Low-current electrical treatment for sweaty palms and soles, in use since the 1950s, with a wider role in drug delivery and diagnostics.
note: Skin irritation possible; effect requires ongoing sessions.
currentQuick:
Iontophoresis passes a weak electric current through water or a drug solution to treat sweaty hands and feet. It was first described for this use in the 1950s, and tap water is commonly used for mild to moderate cases.
It is also used to deliver drugs through skin and for cystic fibrosis sweat testing.
How it works: The current moves charged molecules across the skin's outer layer, and the resulting effects temporarily reduce sweat output.
Risks and caveats: Skin irritation or burns are possible if current density is too high; Grokipedia also notes cost and the need for charged substances.
deepLead:
Iontophoresis is a method of delivering substances through the skin using a low-intensity electric current, with charged molecules moved across the skin by electrorepulsion and electro-osmosis . In grooming and dermatology it is mainly known as a treatment for excessive sweating of the palms and soles (palmar-plantar hyperhidrosis) .
Wikipedia states that tap water is often used for mild and moderate cases and that a glycopyrronium or glycopyrrolate solution may be used for severe cases . The use for hyperhidrosis was first described in the 1950s, and one trial reportedly found about an 80% reduction in sweating .
Iontophoresis also has diagnostic uses, notably pilocarpine iontophoresis to induce sweat for cystic fibrosis testing .

name: Armpit shaving

chain: Less surface for sweat and bacteria
angle.text: Shaving the underarms gives a smooth, groomed look at once and is proposed in looksmaxxing circles as a way to cut odor held by hair. The one study found shaved and unshaved armpits smelled the same.

summary: Shaving the pits to cut odor-holding hair; the one study found shaved and unshaved smelled the same.
note: Razor irritation; shared barber equipment has been linked to hepatitis C transmission in Pakistan.
currentQuick:
Armpit shaving removes underarm hair with a razor. Some in grooming communities do it hoping to reduce odor, reasoning that hair holds sweat and bacteria.
The evidence is thin. A 2012 study cited on Wikipedia reported that shaved and unshaved armpits were rated as smelling the same.
How it works: A razor cuts the hair at the skin surface, and regrowth occurs within days. Odor itself comes from bacteria acting on apocrine sweat.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include skin irritation, increased absorption of deodorant chemicals through damaged skin, and, with shared unsterilised barber tools, infection transmission.
deepLead:
Armpit shaving is the removal of underarm hair at the skin surface with a razor. It is the most common form of hair removal in general, and its results last only hours to days. In looksmaxxing and grooming discussions it is proposed as a way to reduce body odor, on the reasoning that hair gives bacteria and sweat more surface to cling to.
Body odor in the armpit arises mainly when skin bacteria such as Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus break down secretions from apocrine sweat glands. One study cited on Wikipedia's underarm hair page reported that shaved and unshaved armpits were rated as smelling the same. Published evidence on the topic is limited.

name: Pit hair laser removal

angle.text: Laser hair removal gives lasting smooth underarms, and is discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a lasting way to reduce armpit odor by removing hair. The hair reduction is visible; the odor benefit is untested.

summary: Laser to remove armpit hair for good; it cuts hair, but odor benefit is untested.
note: No studies of odor outcomes; side effects reported as temporary.
currentQuick:
Underarm laser hair removal damages hair follicles with light. Some people pursue it hoping for lasting odor reduction.
Studies show hair reduction, about half for up to six months with alexandrite or diode lasers, but none found test odor.
How it works: Light is absorbed by dark hair pigment and damages the follicle.
Risks and caveats: Reported side effects are temporary, and were more frequent with diode lasers than alexandrite or intense pulsed light in one 2006 comparison.
deepLead:
Laser hair removal uses light absorbed by dark pigment to damage hair follicles. It has been FDA-approved in the US since 1997 and became widespread from the 1990s. Underarms are one area treated, and in looksmaxxing circles the procedure is discussed as a lasting way to reduce armpit odor by removing the hair.
A 2006 meta-analysis described on Wikipedia found alexandrite and diode lasers reduced hair by about 50 percent for up to six months, with no evidence of benefit from intense pulsed light, Nd:YAG, or ruby lasers. The sources reviewed contain no studies of laser hair removal specifically for body odor.

name: Acid body wash (AHA/BHA) for pits

chain: Acid exfoliates and lowers skin pH
angle.text: Users apply AHA or BHA washes to the armpits on the theory that lower pH and removal of dead skin starves odor bacteria. The idea is plausible chemically but untested for odor.

summary: AHA/BHA exfoliating wash on the pits to starve odor bacteria; plausible in theory, untested for odor.
note: Can irritate and raise sunburn likelihood.
currentQuick:
Acid body washes use AHAs or BHA to exfoliate. Some people use them on the armpits hoping to reduce odor.
No studies were found testing this use.
How it works: Acids loosen dead skin cells. Proponents say this plus a lower surface pH disfavors odor bacteria.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects are mild irritation, redness and flaking, plus increased sunburn likelihood per FDA caution.
deepLead:
Acid body washes contain alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) such as glycolic or lactic acid, or beta hydroxy acid (BHA, salicylic acid), which chemically exfoliate skin. In looksmaxxing discussions they are applied to the armpits on the theory that lowering skin pH and removing dead skin reduces odor-causing bacteria.
AHAs are used in cosmetics to exfoliate, and the most common effects are mild irritation, redness and flaking. No studies of acid washes for underarm odor were found among the sources reviewed.

name: Benzoyl peroxide wash for body odor

angle.text: An acne wash repurposed for armpits and body, used on the theory that it kills odor-producing bacteria. Its antibacterial role in acne is established, while its use for odor is untested.

summary: Acne antibacterial wash repurposed for pit odor; the mechanism is plausible but odor use is untested.
note: Irritation, photosensitivity and permanent fabric bleaching.
currentQuick:
Benzoyl peroxide washes are acne products that some people use on the armpits to reduce odor.
Wikipedia does not mention body odor use, and no studies were found testing it.
How it works: For acne it kills bacteria by oxidative damage; proponents extend this to odor bacteria.
Risks and caveats: Irritation is common, about 1 in 500 have hypersensitivity, phototoxicity occurs, and it can permanently bleach fabrics and towels.
deepLead:
Benzoyl peroxide is an oxidizer used mainly as an acne medication. It is sold over the counter and appears on the WHO list of essential medicines. In looksmaxxing and body-care discussions, benzoyl peroxide washes are applied to the armpits or body on the theory that they kill odor-producing bacteria.
Wikipedia's article does not mention body odor. For acne, the compound is thought to kill Cutibacterium acnes through oxidative damage, reduce sebum and unclog pores. No studies of benzoyl peroxide for underarm odor were found.

name: Antibacterial soap (Hibiclens)

angle.text: Hibiclens, a hospital chlorhexidine antiseptic wash, is used by looksmaxxing posters on underarms to reduce odor-causing bacteria. Its antibacterial action is established; odor outcomes have not been tested.

summary: Hospital chlorhexidine antiseptic wash used for pit odor; strong antibacterial, odor outcomes untested.
note: Must avoid eyes and ears.
currentQuick:
Hibiclens is a chlorhexidine antiseptic wash. Some use it on the armpits to cut odor-causing bacteria.
It is well established as a medical skin antiseptic; no studies were found testing it for cosmetic body odor.
How it works: Chlorhexidine binds bacterial cell walls, stopping growth or killing bacteria depending on concentration.
Risks and caveats: Skin irritation, allergic reactions, and eye or inner-ear toxicity.
deepLead:
Hibiclens is a brand of topical chlorhexidine skin cleanser, one of several chlorhexidine brands. Chlorhexidine is an antiseptic used to prepare skin before surgery, clean wounds and in surgical scrubs, and is sold over the counter in the US. In looksmaxxing and body-care discussions it is used as a body wash for underarm odor, on the idea that it reduces odor-causing skin bacteria.
In hospitals, daily bathing of intensive care patients with chlorhexidine-soaked washcloths reduced hospital-acquired infections in one US trial. Studies of chlorhexidine for cosmetic body odor were not found.

name: Zinc-based deodorant (Zinc ricinoleate)

angle.text: Zinc ricinoleate, a castor-oil zinc salt, is added to deodorants as an odor-adsorbing ingredient and mentioned as an alternative to aluminium antiperspirants. The mechanism is unclear and no trials were found.

summary: Castor-oil zinc salt in deodorants that claims to adsorb odor; mechanism unclear, no trials.
note: Safety data not found in reviewed sources.
currentQuick:
Zinc ricinoleate is an ingredient in many deodorants, where it is described as adsorbing odor rather than masking it.
Its mechanism is described as unclear, and no clinical studies were found.
How it works: Said to bind odor molecules; a 2000 simulation study examined the adsorption.
Risks and caveats: Safety information was not found in the reviewed sources.
deepLead:
Zinc ricinoleate is the zinc salt of ricinoleic acid, a main fatty acid in castor oil. Many deodorants include it as an odor-adsorbing ingredient, meaning it is said to capture odor molecules rather than mask them or stop sweat. In looksmaxxing and grooming discussions it is mentioned as an alternative to aluminum antiperspirants.
Wikipedia states that the mechanism of this activity is unclear. No clinical studies of zinc ricinoleate deodorants were found.

name: Mandelic acid deodorant (Lume)

angle.text: Mandelic acid deodorants, best known through Lume, use an acid-based formula instead of aluminium to control odor. The chemistry is plausible, but no deodorant trials exist.

summary: An acid-based deodorant built on mandelic acid, made popular by Lume; plausible chemistry but no deodorant trials exist.
note: No clinical trials of mandelic acid for odour; acids can irritate underarm skin.
currentQuick:
Mandelic acid deodorants use an alpha hydroxy acid instead of aluminium salts to manage underarm and body odour. Lume is the best-known brand and sells it as a whole body deodorant.
The ingredient has a long record in chemical peels, but no published study has tested it as a deodorant.
How it works: Body odour comes from skin bacteria breaking down apocrine sweat. Acid-based deodorants are described as keeping the skin surface acidic so bacteria grow less; they do not reduce sweating.
Risks and caveats: Acids can irritate skin, and underarm skin is sensitive. Deodorants are regulated as cosmetics in the US. No product-specific safety trials were located.
deepLead:
Mandelic acid deodorant refers to underarm and body deodorants built around mandelic acid, an aromatic alpha hydroxy acid, rather than around aluminium salts or fragrance. The best-known example is Lume, a brand that markets a "whole body" deodorant and describes the acid-based formula as an odour-control product.
Mandelic acid was first isolated in 1831 from bitter almond extract and is widely used in superficial chemical peels and as a pharmaceutical precursor. Body odour arises mainly when skin bacteria break down secretions from apocrine sweat glands, which is the process acid-based deodorants are intended to interfere with.
No published clinical trials were found that test mandelic acid deodorants for odour control. The wiki therefore records the product category mainly through its manufacturer's claims and the general chemistry and dermatology of the ingredient.

name: Lume whole body deodorant

angle.text: Lume is a viral acid-based deodorant sold for the whole body, discussed on short-video platforms as a non-aluminium option. Its popularity is clear; it has not been tested in trials.

summary: A viral acid-based deodorant sold for the whole body; popular, but untested in trials.
note: No clinical trials; acid products can irritate skin.
currentQuick:
Lume is a deodorant brand marketing a mandelic acid formula for the whole body rather than just the underarms. It gained attention on short-video platforms.
No published study has tested it, so claims rest on the manufacturer and user reports.
How it works: It is a deodorant, so it targets odour-causing bacteria rather than sweat. Acid-based products are described as keeping skin mildly acidic.
Risks and caveats: Possible skin irritation, particularly on sensitive or freshly shaved skin. Regulated as a cosmetic in the US; no product-specific safety trials were found.
deepLead:
Lume is a deodorant brand that markets a "whole body" deodorant, intended for use beyond the underarms, built on an acid-based formula using mandelic acid. The product became widely discussed on short-video platforms, and is the best-known example of a wider trend toward non-aluminium, acid-based deodorants.
As a deodorant, it is aimed at odour rather than sweat. Body odour arises mainly from bacteria breaking down secretions of the apocrine sweat glands, concentrated in the armpits. In the US, deodorants are regulated as cosmetics, while antiperspirants are regulated as drugs.
Source material for this entry is limited to the manufacturer's site and general reference works. No published clinical trials of Lume were found.

name: Magnesium deodorant

angle.text: Magnesium hydroxide deodorants, including milk of magnesia, are used as natural aluminium-free options for underarm odor. They are popular, but no trials were found.

summary: An aluminium-free deodorant using magnesium hydroxide; popular as a natural alternative, but no trials exist.
note: No clinical studies; does not reduce sweat.
currentQuick:
Magnesium deodorants use magnesium hydroxide, the ingredient in milk of magnesia, as an aluminium-free way to manage underarm odour.
No published trials were found, and reference sources only briefly mention the use.
How it works: They act on odour, not sweating. Odour comes from bacteria breaking down apocrine sweat; magnesium products are generally described as mildly alkaline odour reducers.
Risks and caveats: Magnesium hydroxide is labelled as a mild skin, eye and respiratory irritant in bulk. Oral overuse can cause diarrhoea. No product-specific safety studies were found.
deepLead:
Magnesium deodorant refers to aluminium-free deodorants that use a magnesium compound, most often magnesium hydroxide (the active in milk of magnesia), applied to the underarms to reduce odour. Wikipedia's deodorant article notes that milk of magnesia is sometimes used this way, and that some versions contain trace sodium hypochlorite, a bactericide.
Magnesium hydroxide is a poorly soluble white solid used mainly as an antacid and, at higher oral doses, an osmotic laxative. Its deodorant use is not well documented in the reference literature: the Wikipedia article on magnesium hydroxide lists it as an antiperspirant component with no supporting citation.
No clinical studies of magnesium deodorants were found.

name: Crystal deodorant (alum stone)

chain: Alum salt rubbed on damp skin
angle.text: Alum stones are rubbed on skin as a natural, fragrance-free deodorant with ancient use. Published evidence is limited to irritation case reports, so odor control rests on tradition and anecdote.

summary: A block of alum rubbed on skin as a natural deodorant; ancient use, but published evidence is limited to irritation case reports.
note: Case reports of irritant and granulomatous dermatitis; still an aluminium compound.
currentQuick:
Crystal deodorant is a block of potassium or ammonium alum, rubbed on damp skin to reduce odour. Alum has been used for centuries, and powdered alum is a traditional deodorant in Southeast Asia.
No controlled trials of its effectiveness were found; the published literature is mostly case reports of skin reactions.
How it works: Alum is astringent and is described as inhibiting the bacterial action that causes underarm odour. It does not block sweat like antiperspirants.
Risks and caveats: Case reports describe irritant dermatitis and granulomatous dermatitis in the armpits. Alum is an aluminium compound, though a different form from antiperspirant salts.
deepLead:
Crystal deodorant, often sold as an alum stone or "rock crystal", is a block of potassium or ammonium alum, a hydrated double sulfate salt of aluminium, rubbed on damp skin to reduce underarm and foot odour. It is marketed as a natural, fragrance-free alternative to conventional deodorants.
Alum has been used since antiquity, as a dye mordant and as a styptic, and in Island Southeast Asia powdered potassium alum (tawas) is a traditional scentless deodorant. Despite being sold as aluminium-free in some marketing, alum is an aluminium compound, though chemically different from the aluminium salts in antiperspirants.
Published literature on the products consists mainly of case reports of skin reactions, including irritant dermatitis and granulomatous dermatitis. No controlled trials of effectiveness were found.
